Ashleigh Harding and Katelyn Grimson | EIT Accounting Graduates at BDO Gisborne

From classroom learning to thriving careers, EIT accounting graduates making their mark at BDO Gisborne.

We’re proud to share this kōrero featuring Kylee Potae, Advisory Director and Managing Partner at BDO Gisborne, alongside EIT Bachelor of Accounting graduates Ashleigh Harding and Katelyn Grimson.

In this video, Kylee talks about why BDO loves welcoming EIT graduates into their team, because of ‘their vibrant, their young, their energetic, they’ve got great skills and they bring a good positive energy’. Katelyn gives us a glimpse into her day to day mahi preparing financial accounts and supporting clients, while Ashleigh reflects on the incredible study support, she received from BDO as she completed both her EIT degree and the Chartered Accountancy Programme.

Their journeys show just how far a qualification in accounting can take you, from hands on learning at EIT to meaningful work in a supportive, future focused firm.

If you’re someone who loves problem solving, numbers, and helping people succeed, this pathway could be your next big step.

GIS Micro-Credential Course Overview with SIT and Māori GIS Resources

This Ngā Poutama Matawhenua webinar introduces the Geographic Information Systems micro-credential offered by the Southern Institute of Technology. The session is aimed at iwi, hapū, Māori organisations, trusts, and whānau who are interested in gaining practical GIS knowledge that can support mahi across whenua, taiao, planning, and environmental kaupapa.
Programme Manager Jordon Traill from SIT explains how the micro-credential works, the skills that are taught, and how the course can fit alongside full time mahi. The course is delivered using a HyFlex approach, allowing participation either face to face or online from anywhere around the motu.

The session provides an overview of the course structure, the types of GIS skills that are developed, and how learners can use GIS tools to support mapping, spatial analysis, and decision making for kaupapa Māori.

Following the main session, our facilitator Duane Wilkins shares a couple of resource sites that could be useful in assisting your GIS Mapping journey.

Kete Aronui: GIS Mapping to Support Kauri and Ngahere Health

This wānanga explores Kete Aronui, a GIS mapping system developed to support Tiakina Kauri (https://www.kauriprotection.co.nz/) and key kauri protection mahi in partnership with mana whenua and collaborating agencies. Kete Aronui enables iwi, councils, Department of Conservation (DOC) and forest groups to collect, manage, and visualise kauri-related data in a safe and secure way.

This is a hands-on demo using test data to show how the system works in the ngahere, in the office, and across Aotearoa.

What you will see
● Field data collection using ArcGIS mobile tools for kauri health mahi
● Data security using group membership and permissions
● Controlled visibility at ngahere partnership levels
● Web-based visualisation and analysis, including points, host population maps, imagery, and contextual layers like rivers, tracks, and contours
● A practical approach that supports kaitiakitanga while each group keeps control over its own data

New Zealand's electricity infrastructure

We’re going to need 80% more electricity by 2050! Watch 'Volt' explain how we’re planning to do this.

Takapu Road Substation - 2025 Planting Day

Transpower AUFLS transition project

You can't always stop something bad from happening, but you can make sure you're able to prevent the bad things from getting exponentially worse. 

For us in our role operating New Zealand's complex power system, this looks like having smart tools and processes for all situations so that we can handle system events and avoid blackouts. 

One critical tool that meets this definition is our Automatic Under-frequency Load Shedding Scheme (AUFLS), which serves to keep the system's voltage and frequency stable during times when it drops dangerously low.  

It does this by instantly acting to reduce load on the system in a planned way by disconnecting power to certain areas. Although this means a short power cut from some, it prevents a more widespread and longer lasting outage that could take days to restore. 

Fortunately, AUFLS has only been used a few times in the past, but we recently worked with industry to transition to a new design that further enhances system security in case we need to call on it in the future. 

A massive thanks to our partners across the sector who were involved in this important mahi that's helped us all be in a better position to handle challenges thrown our way.

ASB Good as Gold: Stu Brickland

This week's ASB Good as Gold recipient is Stu Brickland of Pukehina. 

He is the driving force behind a community initiative that has gone from a few mates and their classic cars to one of the Bay of Plenty’s most anticipated annual events. A long-time local, Stu helped establish the Pukehina Surf'n'Sand Autorama with all proceeds supporting the local Surf Life Saving Club and Volunteer Fire Brigade. Now attracting more than 500 vehicles and over 10,000 visitors each year, the event has outgrown its original park and moved to school grounds and neighbouring paddocks. A full-time plumber, Stu is known for always making time to help others, quietly giving back wherever he can. 

Thanks to his commitment and leadership, more than $150,000 has been returned to the Pukehina community over four years, allowing the supported organisations to purchase essential equipment to keep the community safe. ASB is proud to recognise Stu as this week’s ASB Good as Gold recipient with $10,000.

ASB Good as Gold: Harry Andrew

This week's ASB Good as Gold recipient is Harry Andrew of Ōamaru. 

Harry's passion for trains began at five years old, and over the years, he has transformed this love into action by establishing Ōamaru's heritage railway, Ōamaru Steam and Rail. Harry has not only restored vintage locomotives and carriages but also mentored over 30 young students, guiding them to become drivers, guards, and mechanics. Harry's hands-on dedication is evident in his single-handed restoration of locomotives and leadership of volunteers in additional projects, many now regularly in use. His current project is restoring a 1946 DM16 Railcar, personally funded and set for unveiling in March 2026. 

His quiet humility and tireless efforts have preserved a rich heritage for Ōamaru, which ASB is honoured to celebrate with $10,000 as this week's ASB Good as Gold recipient.

Transpower AUFLS transition project

You can't always stop something bad from happening, but you can make sure you're able to prevent the bad things from getting exponentially worse. 

For us in our role operating New Zealand's complex power system, this looks like having smart tools and processes for all situations so that we can handle system events and avoid blackouts. 

One critical tool that meets this definition is our Automatic Under-frequency Load Shedding Scheme (AUFLS), which serves to keep the system's voltage and frequency stable during times when it drops dangerously low.  

It does this by instantly acting to reduce load on the system in a planned way by disconnecting power to certain areas. Although this means a short power cut from some, it prevents a more widespread and longer lasting outage that could take days to restore. 

Fortunately, AUFLS has only been used a few times in the past, but we recently worked with industry to transition to a new design that further enhances system security in case we need to call on it in the future. 

A massive thanks to our partners across the sector who were involved in this important mahi that's helped us all be in a better position to handle challenges thrown our way.

Home Sweet Home

This project expanded on the BJ Ball student design contest ‘Home Sweet Home’ which asked ākonga to design a typographical poster describing what ‘your home’ means to them. Ākonga developed three short phrases describing their perceptions of home and rendered these phrases in three different styles. Ākonga also investigated different typographic and animation techniques to create short, animated versions of their phrases. Their final posters were selected and refined from their animations and submitted to the BK Ball Home Sweet Home competition.

Bubble Tea

Motion graphics transforms static design into dynamic visual storytelling. In this project, ākonga created an engaging promotional video for a hypothetical bubble tea café, using animated typography and abstract shapes to express the brand’s energy and appeal. Guided by motion design principles – such as timing, squash & stretch, ease, arcs, emphasis, contrast, scale, and rhythm – they crafted vibrant visuals designed to resonate with the intended target audience.

Jasmine Hay, Seungbeom Son, Sophia Jones, Toby Kilford, Torridon Stallworthy, Meruert Omarkhanova, Grace Huang, Awhina Anderson, Junior Fetoai, Brant Foesther, Jayden Yap, Sam Maddocks, Shalom Pikari, Jasper Theodorou, Lia Vaamailalo

Urban Jungle

In this project, ākonga created looping animated collages by blending photographic imagery with creative elements. Using After Effects, they designed three dynamic scenes, leveraging 3D space and animating a camera through each one. A selected object acted as a portal, seamlessly linking each scene. Ākonga explored ways to weave together their photographic imagery with colour, shape and text to visually express the essence of ‘the urban jungle’ in their animations. 

Awhina Anderson, Maxine Campbell, Luka Craig, Junior Fetoai, Sadie Greenslade, Sam Maddocks, Cam Thomson, Lia Vaamailalo 

Bachelor of Creativity Level 5: Screen Design 1 

Urban Jungle: Motion Graphics, (2025)

Horse in Motion

The Horse in Motion (1878), photographed by Eadweard Muybridge, is an iconic sequence and one of the earliest examples of capturing movement frame by frame – predating modern film. In this exercise, ākonga used these individual frames from this sequence as a reference to create a rotoscoped animation, using both hand-rendered and digital techniques to bring motion to life.
